Skipping what is not needed

The fastest way to read a big file is to not read most of it. A file has several levels of information that tell a reader what a part of it holds, and a ParquetFilter is checked against them:

Level What it records Written by default Rules out
Row group statistics the smallest and largest value of each column of the row group, and how many are null yes whole row groups
Page index the same for every page of a column, and where the page is no (WritePageIndex) pages inside a row group
Bloom filters whether a value is certainly not in the column of a row group no (ColumnBloomFilters) row groups, for equality conditions
Page checksums a CRC-32 of every page no (WritePageChecksums) nothing: they detect damaged pages

Filters

using ParquetNeo;

var recent = ParquetFilter.Column("Born").GreaterThanOrEqual(new DateOnly(1900, 1, 1))
           & ParquetFilter.Column("Name").IsNotNull();

A filter is made of comparisons (Equal, NotEqual, GreaterThan, ..., Between, In), null tests, and And (&), Or (|) and Not (!).

Important

A filter only prunes. It rules out what cannot match, and the rows of what it keeps are all returned, including rows that do not satisfy it. Apply the condition to the rows as well when the result must be exact. (ParquetNeo.Linq does that for you.)

Using them

var rows = ParquetSerializer.Deserialize<Person>(stream, new ParquetDeserializerOptions { RowGroupFilter = recent });

ParquetDataReaderOptions.RowGroupFilter is the same for the ADO.NET reader, and ParquetFileReader.GetMatchingRowGroups(filter) tells you which row groups of a file may match.

The row groups that are ruled out are not read. The asynchronous methods of ParquetSerializer do not even fetch their bytes, but they only use the statistics: they do not fetch the page index or the bloom filters.

The page index

A row group is made of many pages, and its statistics say nothing of which of them hold a value. With a page index, a filter skips pages as well as row groups:

var options = new ParquetSerializerOptions { Writer = new ParquetWriterOptions { WritePageIndex = true } };

It pays when the values of a column are in some order (a time, an id that grows), which makes the bounds of a page tight. Reading 100 ids out of 2 million in one row group took 313 ms with the statistics of the row group only and 39 ms with the page index (158 and 48 ms with gzip). The index took 2.5 KB of a 63 MB file, and writing took 8 to 10% longer.

At the low level, RowGroupReader.SelectRows(filter, columns) returns the rows to read as a RowSelection, and OpenColumn(index, selection) reads only those rows: the pages with none of them are not read.

Bloom filters

Statistics rule out little when values are spread widely (ids, names, e-mail addresses): every row group has a smallest and a largest value that bracket what you look for. A bloom filter says that a value is certainly not in a row group, or that it may be (with a small chance of a wrong "may be", the false positive rate).

var written = new ParquetSerializerOptions
{
    Writer = new ParquetWriterOptions
    {
        ColumnBloomFilters = new Dictionary<string, BloomFilterSettings> { ["Email"] = new() { FalsePositiveRate = 0.01 } },
    },
};

var found = ParquetSerializer.Deserialize<Person>(stream, new ParquetDeserializerOptions
{
    RowGroupFilter = ParquetFilter.Column("Email").Equal("ada@example.com"),
});

A filter takes room in the file: about a byte for every few different values. Writing the column takes several times as long when its pages are not compressed, and a little longer when they are. Bloom filters in files written by other tools are read too.

Page checksums

var written = new ParquetWriterOptions { WritePageChecksums = true };
var read = new ParquetReaderOptions { VerifyPageChecksums = true };   // a damaged page throws CorruptColumnException

Computing the checksum costs about a second per GB of page bytes.
